summary.text: A galaxy rotation curve is a plot of how fast a galaxy's visible stars or gas orbit, set against their distance from the galaxy's centre.
Outside the central bulge, observed curves are flat, with nearly constant speed, instead of falling with distance as Newtonian mechanics would predict.
Dark matter is by far the most accepted explanation of this mismatch, with modified Newtonian dynamics the most notable alternative.

items.prompt: In our Solar System, planets far from the Sun move more slowly than close ones. If a galaxy behaved the same way, what would its outer stars do?

options.label: Speed up steadily with distance
Orbit at a constant speed whatever their distance
Orbit more slowly with distance from the centre
Stop moving once they leave the bulge

items.explain: If Newtonian mechanics holds and most mass is in the central bulge, stars and gas should orbit at decreasing velocities with distance from the centre.

items.prompt: Astronomers measure many spiral galaxies and plot the speed of stars far from the centre. What do they find?

options.label: Speeds fall off quickly, as expected
The speed of the stars is nearly constant outside the bulge
The outer stars are not moving at all
Speeds reach a peak and then drop to zero

items.explain: The curves are flat: outside the central bulge the speed is nearly constant, rather than falling as expected.

items.prompt: A galaxy's mass is estimated from the light it gives off, and its stars still orbit too fast. What does this say about the light-based estimate?

options.label: It is far too low to explain the observed speeds
It is correct and the speeds must be wrong
It is too high compared with the speeds
It cannot be compared with any speeds

items.explain: Mass estimates based on the light that galaxies emit are far too low to explain the velocity observations.

items.prompt: The flat curves cannot be explained by the stars we see. What could account for them?

options.label: More bright stars packed into the central bulge
A stronger pull on the outer stars from the Sun
Dim matter spread through the galaxy outside the bulge
A slower spin than the one we measured

items.explain: The curves might be explained by a substantial amount of matter permeating the galaxy outside the central bulge that is not emitting light like the bulge.

items.prompt: Horace Babcock found fast rotation in Andromeda's outer parts. How did he explain it?

options.label: Missing matter was holding the galaxy together
Light absorbed inside the galaxy or modified dynamics in the outer spiral
Mistakes made by using an old instrument
A second galaxy hidden behind Andromeda

items.explain: He attributed it to light absorption inside the galaxy or modified dynamics in the outer spiral, and not to any form of missing matter.

items.prompt: Oort studied NGC 3115 and found that its mass looked unrelated to its light. What ratio of mass to light did he find in the outer parts?

options.label: About 1, as bright as expected
About 10, a little above normal
About 50, well above the normal value
About 250, far above what light suggests

items.explain: Oort found the ratio of mass to light in the outer parts of NGC 3115 to be about 250, with mass bearing almost no relation to light.

paragraphs.heading: Speed against distance
paragraphs.text: A rotation curve, also called a velocity curve, is a graph for a disc galaxy. It shows how fast the visible stars or gas are orbiting, plotted against how far they sit from the galaxy's centre. The two sides of a spiral galaxy usually do not match, so astronomers average them to draw one curve.

paragraphs.heading: What gravity predicts
paragraphs.text: If Newton's laws of motion are correct, it seems to follow that most of a galaxy's mass should sit in the central bulge. Then stars and gas farther out in the disc should orbit more and more slowly the farther they are from the middle. Real curves do not do this. Outside the bulge they stay flat: the orbital speed is nearly the same at every distance.

paragraphs.heading: A mass that light misses
paragraphs.text: So the measured curves clash with gravity applied to the visible matter. The amount of mass you would guess from a galaxy's light is far too small to account for the speeds. The main proposed answer is dark matter: a large amount of matter spread through the galaxy beyond the bulge that gives off much less light for its mass than the bulge does. Other ideas exist, the best known being modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND), which changes the laws of gravity.

paragraphs.heading: Early measurements
paragraphs.text: Vesto Slipher took the first related measurements in 1914, looking at the Andromeda galaxy. Stars on one side of its bulge were coming toward us at around 320 km/s, faster than those on the other side at about 280 km/s, which hinted the disc was spinning. In 1957 Henk van de Hulst and colleagues used a new 25-meter radio telescope at Dwingeloo to measure an extended curve for M31 that agrees well with modern data. A companion paper by Maarten Schmidt showed the curve fit a flattened spread of mass reaching farther than the light.

paragraphs.heading: Rubin and Ford
paragraphs.text: In the late 1960s and early 1970s, Vera Rubin worked with a new, sensitive spectrograph that measured the velocity curves of edge-on spiral galaxies more accurately than ever. In 1975 she and Kent Ford announced that most stars in spiral galaxies orbit at about the same speed. That meant a galaxy's mass keeps growing roughly in step with radius, well past where most of its stars are. Either Newtonian gravity does not apply everywhere, or more than half of a galaxy's mass lies in a dim halo. Doubted at first, her results have been confirmed in the decades since.

paragraphs.heading: A ruler from rotation
paragraphs.text: Rotation also links to brightness through the Tully–Fisher relation. For spiral galaxies, the rotation speed is tied to how luminous the galaxy is overall. Measure one and you can read off the other from the Tully–Fisher diagram. So how fast a galaxy turns is connected to how much visible mass it has.
